question: Is LVP or tile the smarter choice for a long-term rental property?
title: LVP or Tile: Smarter Choice for a Rental Property?
h1: Is LVP or Tile the Smarter Pick for a Long-Term Rental?
description: 20-mil LVP runs $2.75-$5.50/sq ft installed vs $6-$10 for porcelain tile in 2026. Here's which holds up better between tenants and why.
capsule: For a long-term Florida rental, 20-mil rigid-core LVP typically installs for $2.75-$5.50 per square foot versus roughly $6-$10 for 12-18 inch porcelain tile, per local 2026 ranges. LVP is cheaper and faster to replace between tenants; tile lasts longer under heavy traffic but costs more up front and takes longer to redo.

sections.h2: Cost Per Square Foot: What Landlords Actually Pay
sections.html:
Our typical 2026 local ranges put mid-range 20-mil SPC LVP at $2.75-$5.50 per square foot installed, against $6-$10 per square foot for 12-18 inch porcelain tile. That gap adds up fast across a multi-unit property, which is why LVP tends to be the default for landlords managing several units on a budget.

Material cost is only part of the picture for a landlord running several units. Ordering the same LVP product across multiple properties also simplifies inventory, if a plank gets damaged in unit 3, the same box of spare material works for unit 7, which isn't true if every unit has a different tile pattern. We can usually source the same LVP line consistently for a year or two before a manufacturer changes a run, which matters if you're trying to keep flooring consistent across a growing portfolio.

sections.h2: Wear and Tear: What Holds Up Between Tenants
sections.html:
Tile's durability is rated on the PEI scale, which runs 0 to 5: PEI 2 suits light traffic like bathrooms and bedrooms, PEI 3 covers all residential floors, and PEI 4 handles heavy residential to medium commercial use, the range most rental common areas fall into. For LVP, wear-layer thickness plays a similar role; a 20-mil wear layer is the usual commercial-grade minimum, recommended over the standard 12-mil for rentals with regular tenant turnover.

Pets are the wildcard in this comparison. A dog's claws can scratch even a 20-mil wear layer over years of daily use, while tile's hard surface resists scratching almost entirely, though a dropped bowl or a slid piece of furniture can chip it. Neither material is scratch-proof; they just fail differently. If scratching is your main concern, ask about a matte or textured LVP finish, which hides light surface wear better than a high-gloss finish does.

A two-person crew can lay about 1,000 square feet of click LVP in one to two days on a ready slab, while tile needs 24 hours before grouting and up to 72 hours before heavy loads return. If speed between leases matters more than upfront durability, that gap favors LVP; we cover both timelines in more depth in separate posts on fast turnarounds and whole-house timelines.

Vacancy carries a real cost for a landlord; every extra day a unit sits empty for flooring work is a day without rent coming in. That's the practical reason speed matters here beyond simple convenience, and it's a bigger factor for a single-unit landlord than for one managing a large portfolio with staggered lease dates.

For turnover-heavy properties where cost and speed matter most, we typically lean toward 20-mil LVP. For common areas or units with pets prone to scratching floors, tile's higher PEI rating holds up longer despite the higher upfront cost and slower redo time. There isn't a single right answer across an entire portfolio; it depends on how often you're actually replacing the floor.

A mixed approach works too: LVP throughout the bedrooms and living areas, with tile reserved for kitchens, bathrooms, and entryways where water exposure and heavy foot traffic overlap. That split keeps replacement costs down in the rooms that turn over most often while putting the more durable material where it earns its keep. Bring your unit mix, bedrooms, wet areas, pet policy, to a free in-home estimate and we'll price out a material plan room by room rather than one blanket recommendation.

faqs.q: Does tile really last longer than LVP for rentals?
faqs.a: Generally yes under heavy traffic, given a PEI 4 or 5 rating, but grout lines need more cleaning attention between tenants than a click LVP floor does, which is worth weighing against the durability gain.

faqs.q: What PEI rating should a rental's main living area have?
faqs.a: PEI 4 is a reasonable target for heavy residential use; PEI 3 is an acceptable minimum for lower-traffic residential rooms like bedrooms.

faqs.q: Is a 20-mil wear layer enough for a revolving-door rental?
faqs.a: Yes, 20-mil is the usual commercial-grade minimum and the level generally recommended for rentals, large dogs, and kids, well above the standard 12-mil residential wear layer.
